title: Flamingos: Pink Waders
summary: How flamingos wade in shallow salty water, filter food with upside-down beaks, get their pink color from what they eat, live in huge flocks, and visit the coasts of Saudi Arabia.
poll: A flamingo's pink color is its most interesting feature.

versions.title: The Pink Bird
versions.text:
Look at that bird! It is tall and pink. It stands on long, thin legs. It is a flamingo.

This bird likes to wade. It walks in water that is not deep. The water has salt or mud in it.

It eats in a fun way. It puts its head down in the water. Its head is upside down! Its beak is bent. The beak lets the water out. It keeps the food in.

What does it eat? It eats tiny shrimp. It eats tiny plants, too. This food has pink in it. That is what makes the bird pink! A chick is gray at first. It gets pink as it eats.

The bird may stand on one leg. It can rest like that for a long time.

These birds live in a big group. The group is a flock. A flock can have lots and lots of birds.

Each pair makes a nest of mud. They lay one egg on top.

These birds come to Saudi Arabia, too. You can see them on the coast in the cold months.

They live in a big group called a flock. Some flocks have thousands of birds.

Each pair builds a nest out of mud. They lay one egg on top.

These pink birds visit Saudi Arabia, too. In winter, you can see them on the coasts.

Flamingos live in big groups called flocks. Some flocks have thousands of birds.

versions.title: Flamingos: Pink Waders
versions.text:
Picture a tall pink bird balancing in shallow water on legs as thin as sticks. It is a flamingo, one of the most colorful and recognizable birds on Earth, and its unusual habits are just as surprising as its appearance.

Flamingos wade, which means they walk through water that is not very deep. They gather in wetlands, such as salty lakes, lagoons, and muddy coastlines. Because few other animals can survive in such salty conditions, flamingos have abundant food to themselves.

A flamingo feeds in a remarkable way. It lowers its head until it is upside down in the water, and its bent beak functions like a filter. The bird pumps water through the edges of its beak with its thick tongue, so microscopic pieces of food are trapped inside while the water flows back out.

Flamingos consume tiny shrimp and algae, which are simple plant-like organisms. This food contains natural pink coloring that ends up in the bird's feathers, which explains why flamingos are pink. A chick hatches with gray feathers and gradually develops its color as it eats, so a pale adult may simply not be getting enough of the right food.

Flamingos frequently stand on one leg, sometimes for hours at a time. Scientists believe this posture may help them conserve energy, although researchers are still investigating exactly how it works.

Flamingos live in large groups called colonies, and some colonies contain thousands of birds. Being part of a crowd helps protect individuals from predators, because many watchful eyes can spot danger quickly.

Each pair constructs a nest from mud and lays a single egg, and both parents take turns feeding the chick until it is able to find food independently.

Flamingos also visit Saudi Arabia. During winter, people observe them along the coasts of the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, where they wade through the warm, shallow water searching for food.

versions.title: Flamingos: The Pink Waders
versions.text:
Picture a tall pink bird balancing in shallow water on legs as slender as sticks. It is a flamingo, one of the most colorful and recognizable birds on Earth, and its unusual habits are just as surprising as its appearance.

Flamingos wade, which means they walk through water that is relatively shallow. They congregate in wetlands, such as salty lakes, coastal lagoons, and muddy shorelines. Because few other animals can tolerate such salty conditions, flamingos have abundant food with little competition from other species.

A flamingo feeds in a remarkable way. It lowers its head until it is upside down in the water, and its bent beak functions like a filter. The bird pumps water through comb-like plates along the edges of its beak using its muscular tongue, so microscopic food particles are trapped inside while the water escapes.

Flamingos consume tiny shrimp and algae, which are simple plant-like organisms. This food contains natural pigments called carotenoids, which are deposited in the bird's feathers and explain its pink color. A chick hatches with gray feathers and gradually develops its color as it eats, so a pale adult may simply be lacking the right diet.

Flamingos frequently stand on one leg, sometimes for hours at a time. Scientists believe this posture may help them conserve energy, although researchers are still investigating exactly how it works. Interestingly, the joint that appears to be a backward-bending knee is actually the bird's ankle, while the real knee is hidden higher up beneath its feathers.

Flamingos live in large groups called colonies, and some colonies contain thousands of birds, because being part of a crowd helps protect individuals from predators that might attack a lone bird.

Each pair constructs a nest from mud and lays a single egg, and both parents take turns feeding the chick until it is able to find food independently.

Flamingos also visit Saudi Arabia. During winter, people observe them along the coasts of the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, where they wade through warm, shallow water searching for food.

versions.title: Flamingos: The Pink Waders
versions.text:
Picture a tall pink bird balancing gracefully in shallow water on exceptionally slender legs. It is a flamingo, one of the most colorful and recognizable birds on Earth, and its unusual behavior is just as remarkable as its appearance.

Flamingos wade, which means they walk through water that is relatively shallow. They congregate in wetlands, such as salty lakes, coastal lagoons, and muddy shorelines. Because few other animals can tolerate such salty conditions, flamingos enjoy abundant food with very little competition from other species.

A flamingo feeds in an extraordinary way. It lowers its head until it is upside down in the water, and its bent beak functions like a filter. The bird pumps water through comb-like plates along the edges of its beak using its muscular tongue, so microscopic food particles are trapped inside while the water escapes.

Flamingos consume tiny shrimp and algae, which are uncomplicated, plant-like organisms. This food contains natural pigments called carotenoids, which are deposited in the bird's feathers and explain its distinctive pink color. A chick hatches with gray feathers and gradually develops its coloring as it eats, so a pale adult may simply be lacking the appropriate diet.

Flamingos frequently stand on one leg, sometimes for hours at a time. Scientists believe this posture may help them conserve energy, although researchers are still investigating precisely how it works. Interestingly, the joint that appears to be a backward-bending knee is actually the bird's ankle, while the genuine knee is hidden higher up beneath its feathers.

Flamingos live in large groups called colonies, and some colonies contain thousands of birds, because being part of an enormous crowd helps protect individuals from predators that might attack a solitary bird.

Each pair constructs a nest from mud and lays a single egg, and both parents alternate feeding the chick until it is capable of finding food independently.

Biologists currently recognize six species of flamingo, distributed across regions of Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas, and the greater flamingo is both the largest and the most widespread.

Flamingos also visit Saudi Arabia. During winter, observers can find them along the coasts of the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, where they wade through warm, shallow water searching diligently for nourishment.

versions.text:
Visualize a tall, rosy-pink creature balancing gracefully in shallow water on exceptionally slender legs. It is a flamingo, one of the most colorful and immediately recognizable birds on Earth, and its unusual behavior is just as remarkable as its spectacular appearance.

Flamingos wade, which means they walk through water that is relatively shallow. They congregate in wetlands, such as salty lakes, coastal lagoons, and muddy shorelines, because few other animals can tolerate such extremely salty conditions, which allows flamingos to enjoy abundant food with very little competition from other species.

A flamingo feeds in an extraordinary way. It positions its head so it is upside down in the water, and its curved beak functions like a filter. The bird pumps water through comb-like plates along the edges of its beak using its muscular tongue, so microscopic food particles are trapped inside while the water escapes.

Flamingos consume tiny shrimp and algae, which are uncomplicated, plant-like organisms. This diet contains natural pigments called carotenoids, which are gradually deposited in the bird's feathers and produce its distinctive pink coloration. A chick hatches with gray feathers and develops its coloring progressively as it eats, so a pale adult may simply be lacking the appropriate diet.

Flamingos frequently stand on one leg, sometimes for hours at a time. Scientists believe this posture may help them conserve energy, although researchers are still investigating precisely how it works. Interestingly, the joint that appears to be a backward-bending knee is actually the bird's ankle, while the genuine knee is concealed higher up beneath its feathers.

Flamingos live in large groups called colonies, and some colonies contain several thousand individuals, because belonging to an enormous crowd helps protect individuals from predators that might otherwise attack a solitary bird.

Each pair constructs a nest from compacted mud and lays a single egg, and both parents alternate feeding the chick until it is capable of locating food independently.

Biologists currently recognize six separate species of flamingo, distributed across numerous regions of Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas, and the greater flamingo is simultaneously the largest and the most widely distributed.

Flamingos also visit Saudi Arabia. During winter, observers can find them along the coasts of the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, where they wade through warm, shallow water searching diligently for nourishment.
